title: Cricket and the Wiggle-Berry Dust
markdown:
Near the Sunspike Peaks the wind whispered through the pines, and Cricket the goblin was a bundle of moss-green energy. His eyes twinkled with what’s-next, and a smudge of berry juice usually sat on his nose. Ears like tiny green leaves twitched. Today they twitched extra because he had borrowed Uncle Grumbles’ best wizard hat: tall, pointy, midnight-blue velvet dotted with silver stars that shimmered even in daylight. It smelled faintly of moonlight and old paper.

“Just a quick peek into the mountain woods,” he whispered, adjusting the hat. It wobbled and tickled his nose. “A goblin with a wizard hat. This will be grand. Imagine the sights. The smells. Maybe even a dragon.”

He scampered up the rocky path. Pine scent like tiny fragrant fingers. The wind gusted. Tall trees swayed like enormous leafy dancers. The path led to a small clearing by windy cliffs. Crisp air. Damp earth and wild thyme. Two figures were having a loud chat.

“It was right here, Pipwick,” Agnes Honeybloom huffed. Pointy nose. Checked apron. Voice sharp as a dropped pin. She lived in a cozy cottage that was usually a beacon of warmth. Today her voice was sour, like unripe berries.

“But Agnes, my dear woman, I assure you, I placed it on the highest shelf after the dewdrop distillation,” boomed a voice from behind a large sputtering cauldron. Professor Pipwick. His beard was so long it sometimes got caught in his teacup, or worse, his potions. A waterfall of silvery white, often sprinkled with colourful powders.

Cricket peeked from behind a mossy rock. Green skin blended perfectly. They were arguing about something small and sparkly: a tiny vial no bigger than his thumb.

Agnes wrung her hands. Apron crinkled. “That’s where I always keep the Sparkle-Shine dust. The Moonbeam Muffins won’t… well, they won’t sparkle without it.” Her shoulders drooped like wilted flowers. A heavy grey feeling settled in Cricket’s chest, the sort that makes a cottage feel further away.

Pipwick peered into his cauldron. A cloud of purple smoke puffed out, faintly burnt sugar. “And my Grand Elixir of Giggles will simply be a Grumpy Goo without the Glimmer-Granules. They’re practically the same thing, you see, but mine has the… the giggles.” He wiggled his fingers, trying to conjure a giggle. Only a small puff of smoke.

A butterfly doing loop-the-loops in Cricket’s tummy. This was his chance. He would show them how helpful a goblin could be. Especially a goblin wearing a very important-looking hat. He puffed his chest. Midnight-blue velvet rustled.

“Excuse me,” he piped, stepping into the clearing. The wizard and witch jumped. The hat, too big, slid down over his eyes. “I can help.”

“Who… who is that?” Agnes blinked, sharp eyes trying to focus.

“A very small hat-wearing mushroom, perhaps?” Pipwick mused, squinting, spectacles sliding down his nose.

Cricket pushed the hat back with both hands, little green fingers gripping velvet. “I’m Cricket. And I think I know where your Sparkle-Shine dust is.” He remembered a glint earlier, near the base of a twisted old oak whose branches were like gnarled fingers reaching for the sky. He had thought it a shiny stone. He found those near the stream.

“You do?” Agnes looked hopeful. Worry lines softened. Pipwick stroked his beard, thoughtful.

“Yes. Over there.” Cricket pointed a grubby finger and jogged. Little goblin legs, swift. He rummaged among the roots. Not a stone. A little pouch tied with silken thread, shimmering with a faint silvery light. He grabbed it. Heart thumped a drum solo. He raced back, tripped slightly on a stray root, caught himself.

“Here you go,” he declared, holding out the pouch. Pipwick reached, long fingers eager. As Cricket swayed, catching his breath, the wizard hat slipped again. It tumbled from his head and landed with a soft thump right into Agnes’s partially stirred cauldron.

A cloud of shimmering rainbow-coloured dust erupted, surprisingly like fizzy lemonade. It swirled outwards and coated everything: Pipwick’s spectacles, Agnes’s apron, Cricket himself. Instead of making things sparkle, it made them wiggle.

Pipwick’s beard began to dance a jig, each strand independently. Agnes’s checked apron turned polka-dotted and started to sway rhythmically, as if it had a mind of its own. Cricket’s nose suddenly felt as if it were trying to escape his face. It twitched and wriggled uncontrollably.

“Oh, dear,” Pipwick muttered. His beard was now doing a full Charleston, silvery strands a blur.

“My Sparkle-Shine,” Agnes wailed. Her apron was doing a flamenco with an alarming wiggle. “It’s… it’s wiggling.”

Cricket froze. Moss-green eyes wide. Tummy like wobbly jelly. He had tried to help. He had only made things much, much wobblier. The constant wiggling of his nose made it hard to concentrate. He had wanted to impress them. To be the hero of the day. Now he had only made them more cross and more jiggly.

Uncle Grumbles always said a goblin’s best tool is not a pickaxe, it is a thinking cap, even if it is borrowed. Cricket looked at the hat bobbing gently in the now-still cauldron. He looked at Agnes and Pipwick, wiggling awkwardly, movements quite comical. A blush crept up his neck.

He could hide behind a rock. Pretend he had never been there. Let them figure out their wiggling problem. Or he could try to fix this. His borrowed hat had caused the problem. Perhaps it could help solve it too. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a slightly squashed but still delicious-looking berry, deep juicy purple.

“Professor Pipwick,” he said, voice a little shaky and surprisingly steady. “Your Grand Elixir of Giggles needs the Glimmer-Granules, right? And Agnes, your Moonbeam Muffins need Sparkle-Shine dust. What if they aren’t so different after all?”

Pipwick paused his beard’s enthusiastic jig. “Not so different? Poppycock. One is for mirth, the other for muffin marvels.”

“But,” Cricket continued, holding up the berry, wiggling nose forgotten for a moment, “this berry tastes sweet, even though it’s not a mushroom. And this hat,” he gestured to the cauldron, faint shimmers of rainbow dust still clinging to the sides, “made things wiggle. What if the real wonder isn’t just the sparkle, but the joy it brings? The surprise?”

He carefully scooped some of the rainbow dust from the cauldron into a clean leaf he had found. He added a few dewdrops collected from a nearby fern, each a tiny perfect sphere. He stirred with a clean twig and watched the colours swirl.

“This isn’t Sparkle-Shine dust,” he said softly, offering the leaf to Agnes. “And it’s not Glimmer-Granules. It’s wiggle-berry dust. It might not sparkle like you planned, Agnes, but it made your apron dance a jig. And it might not make you giggle like you planned, Professor Pipwick, but it made your beard do a lovely shuffle.”

Agnes looked at her apron. It was still doing a gentle happy shimmy. A tiny smile touched her lips. Pipwick watched his beard settle into a dignified stillness. A rumbling chuckle started in his chest, like distant thunder.

“You know,” Pipwick said, voice warm and rich, eyes crinkling, “the sheer unexpectedness of the jig was quite invigorating. A delightful diversion from the usual boring spells.”

“And my apron is rather cheerful now,” Agnes admitted. A genuine smile. She looked at Cricket. Really looked. Not as a goblin who had made a mess, but as someone who had tried to make things right.

“Perhaps,” she said, taking a pinch of the wiggle-berry dust, pointy nose twitching slightly, “a little bit of wiggling joy is just what a Moonbeam Muffin needs. A dash of surprise.” She sprinkled some on a nearby daisy. The daisy, to everyone’s delight, began to sway gently. Petals danced.

Pipwick nodded. Silvery beard shimmered. “Indeed. A truly novel addition to the Grand Elixir of Giggles. Cricket, my boy, you have a most unconventional, yet brilliant, approach to enchantment.”

Warmth spread through Cricket, much nicer than the ticklish wiggling of his nose. He had not made things sparkle in the way they intended. He had made them smile. He had risked his own embarrassment. He had given up looking like a proper wizard with a grand spell. He had done it for peace, or at least for less wiggling.

The wizard and the witch looked at each other, then at Cricket. A genuine smile bloomed between them and chased away the last traces of their argument. A smile that said they were neighbours again.

“Well,” Agnes said, dusting off her apron, which now seemed to have a cheerful polka-dotted pattern, “it seems we were both a bit too focused on our own recipes. Thank you, Cricket. You’ve reminded us that sometimes the best ingredients for any potion, or any muffin, are a little kindness and a whole lot of understanding.”

Pipwick beamed. “Precisely. And perhaps a touch of unexpected wiggling. It’s the spice of life, wouldn’t you agree?”

Cricket, the young goblin who had borrowed a hat, smiled back. Moss-green eyes shone. He had not managed a grand enchantment. He had brought two grumpy neighbours back together. That felt even better than finding a shiny stone. He scooped the dripping hat from the cauldron, shook off a last rainbow sneeze, and set it back on his head at a slightly braver angle. Uncle Grumbles could have the hat back. Cricket would keep the wiggle.
characters: Cricket (the young goblin), Agnes Honeybloom (checked-apron neighbour)
